body_markdown:
The Web Summit is, without a doubt, one of the world’s premier tech conferences: 800+ speakers, 17 speaking tracks and over 70,000+ attendees – investors, media, startups, VCs and big tech leaders – all gathered in Lisbon, Portugal.


This year’s edition was as big and vibrant as the last time I attended, in 2024, in spite of a cancelled day thanks to the winds and rains of storm Charles. And try as you might, you would have been hard pressed to find a corner of the event that wasn’t talking about AI.


I saw startups selling AI for marketers, personal chief of staff solutions, MCP servers, a website builder for the AI age, facial verification technology for secure building access and an emerging identity-trust management platform. There was even a brand using AI to help gardens flourish, and another for women’s formal dinner wear.


Of most interest to me from a design perspective, there were many physical prototypes showing the acceleration of innovation in robotics – lifelike hands moving in sync with human hands, robots for the household and humanoids showing off their tai chi talents. (I know – we’re not there yet, but it’s definitely moving fast).


I am interested in this, because one topic that preoccupies the design team at the moment is the future of the interface.


For four decades, precision has dominated the interfaces between people and the digital world that we’re all familiar with. Mice point and click. Keyboards and headsets type and talk. Webcams capture and connect.


Now, AI has introduced a second mode: intent. These robots interface with us through a presumed understanding of intent. AI divulges intent. And so, successful innovation today needs to capture and execute on people’s intent, as well as considering precision. They co-exist – often in the same sentence.


I was grateful to be asked to speak on this topic at the Web Summit – how everything in the AI age becomes an interface. AI influences all aspects of interfaces: how we ask, how we confirm, how we stop what we asked for and how we know if the interface is even there.


For example, right now voice is one of the fastest-moving interfaces. It was clunky only a short while ago. Latency issues broke up the natural flow of language. Yet, today you can switch subjects and interrupt a machine in the same way you would do with a colleague. The machine keeps up…


Of course this raises questions about how to interface with machines. Mice and keyboards still remain relevant for focused, precise work. But voice requires a different interface – one that respects the intent and needs of individual users, ITDM choosers, as well as bystanders who might be sitting in an open plan office.


We know a bit about this at Logitech. We’ve been doing it for 45 years. We know that in a world where everything is an interface, control is critical.


Our own research (see


[Logitech’s Ctrl Tomorrow study](https://ctrltomorrow.logitech.com/) ) shows that people who feel in control of their technology get a kind of dividend – improved mood, wellbeing, performance and potential. It’s not just that technology helps them get something done – it improves their experience of life!


The opposite is also true. Someone with the same tech setup might feel out of control with their technology and have the opposite effect – frustration, anxiety, poor wellbeing outcomes.


The challenge – indeed the opportunity – for Logitech in a world where everything is an interface, is to design for control.


This matters more than you might think. The world today is increasingly intangible and fast-moving. AI, for many, feels like a runaway train. Tech moves quickly but human behavior changes slowly. If you can design for control, you help bridge that gap.


That’s what Logitech is all about: extending human potential at work and play.
